L1:---
L2:name: graphify
L3:description: "Use for any question about a codebase, its architecture, file relationships, or project content — especially when graphify-out/ exists, where the question should be treated as a graphify query first. L4:---
L5:
L6:# /graphify
L7:
L8:Turn any folder of files into a navigable knowledge graph with community detection, an honest audit trail, and three outputs: interactive HTML, GraphRAG-ready JSON, and a plain-language GRAPH_REPORT.md.
L9:
L10:## Usage
L11:
L12:```
L13:/graphify                                             # full pipeline on current directory (HTML viz; add --obsidian for a vault)
L14:/graphify <path>                                      # full pipeline on specific path
L15:/graphify https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>           # clone repo then run full pipeline on it
L16:/graphify https://github.com/<owner>/<repo> --branch <branch>  # clone a specific branch
L17:/graphify <url1> <url2> ...                           # clone multiple repos, build each, merge into one cross-repo graph
L18:/graphify <path> --mode deep                          # thorough extraction, richer INFERRED edges
L19:/graphify <path> --update                             # incremental - re-extract only new/changed files
L20:/graphify <path> --directed                            # build directed graph (preserves edge direction: source→target)
L21:/graphify <path> --whisper-model medium                # use a larger Whisper model for better transcription accuracy
L22:/graphify <path> --cluster-only                       # rerun clustering on existing graph
L23:/graphify <path> --no-viz                             # skip visualization, just report + JSON
L24:/graphify <path> --html                               # (HTML is generated by default - this flag is a no-op)
L25:/graphify <path> --svg                                # also export graph.svg (embeds in Notion, GitHub)
L26:/graphify <path> --graphml                            # export graph.graphml (Gephi, yEd)
L27:/graphify <path> --neo4j                              # generate graphify-out/cypher.txt for Neo4j
L28:/graphify <path> --neo4j-push bolt://localhost:7687   # push directly to Neo4j
L29:/graphify <path> --falkordb                           # generate graphify-out/cypher.txt for FalkorDB
L30:/graphify <path> --falkordb-push falkordb://localhost:6379   # push directly to FalkorDB
L31:/graphify <path> --mcp                                # start MCP stdio server for agent access
L32:/graphify <path> --watch                              # watch folder, auto-rebuild on code changes (no LLM needed)
L33:/graphify <path> --wiki                               # build agent-crawlable wiki (index.md + one article per community)
L34:/graphify <path> --obsidian --obsidian-dir ~/vaults/my-project  # write vault to custom path (e.g. existing vault)
L35:/graphify add <url>                                   # fetch URL, save to ./raw, update graph
L36:/graphify add <url> --author "Name"                   # tag who wrote it
L37:/graphify add <url> --contributor "Name"              # tag who added it to the corpus
L38:/graphify query "<question>"                          # BFS traversal - broad context
L39:/graphify query "<question>" --dfs                    # DFS - trace a specific path
L40:/graphify query "<question>" --budget 1500            # cap answer at N tokens
L41:/graphify path "AuthModule" "Database"                # shortest path between two concepts
L42:/graphify explain "SwinTransformer"                   # plain-language explanation of a node
L43:```
L44:
L45:## What graphify is for
L46:
L47:Drop any folder of code, docs, papers, images, or video into graphify and get a queryable knowledge graph. Persistent across sessions, honest audit trail (EXTRACTED/INFERRED/AMBIGUOUS), community detection surfaces cross-document connections you wouldn't think to ask about.
L48:
L49:## What You Must Do When Invoked
L50:
L51:If the user invoked `/graphify --help` or `/graphify -h` (with no other arguments), print the contents of the `## Usage` section above verbatim and stop. Do not run any commands, do not detect files, do not default the path to `.`. Just print the Usage block and return.
L52:
L53:**Fast path — existing graph:** Before doing anything else, check whether `graphify-out/graph.json` exists. The expected location is `graphify-out/graph.json` relative to the **current working directory** (i.e. the project root where you are running commands). If it exists AND the user's request is a natural-language question about the codebase (e.g. "How does X work?", "What calls Y?", "Trace the data flow through Z") and NOT an explicit rebuild command (`--update`, `--cluster-only`, or a bare path/URL that implies fresh extraction): **skip Steps 1–5 entirely and jump straight to `## For /graphify query`.** Run `graphify query "<question>"` immediately. Do not run detect. Do not check corpus size. Do not ask the user to narrow. The graph is already built — use it.
L54:
L55:If no path was given, use `.` (current directory). Do not ask the user for a path.
L56:
L57:If the path argument starts with `https://github.com/` or `http://github.com/`, treat it as a GitHub URL - run Step 0 before anything else, then continue with the resolved local path.
L58:
L59:Follow these steps in order. Do not skip steps.
L60:
L61:### Step 0 - GitHub repos and multi-path merge (only if a URL or several paths)
L62:
L63:Only when the path is one or more `https://github.com/...` URLs, or several local subfolders to merge. See `references/github-and-merge.md` for the clone, cross-repo merge, and monorepo flow, then continue with the resolved local path. A plain local path skips this step.
L64:
L65:### Step 1 - Ensure graphify is installed
L66:
L67:```bash
L68:# Detect the correct Python interpreter (handles uv tool, pipx, venv, system installs)
L69:PYTHON=""
L70:GRAPHIFY_BIN=$(which graphify 2>/dev/null)
L71:# 1. uv tool installs — most reliable on modern Mac/Linux
L72:if [ -z "$PYTHON" ] && command -v uv >/dev/null 2>&1; then
L73:    _UV_PY=$(uv tool run --from graphifyy python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)" 2>/dev/null)
L74:    if [ -n "$_UV_PY" ]; then PYTHON="$_UV_PY"; fi
L75:fi
L76:# 2. Read shebang from graphify binary (pipx and direct pip installs)
L77:if [ -z "$PYTHON" ] && [ -n "$GRAPHIFY_BIN" ]; then
L78:    _SHEBANG=$(head -1 "$GRAPHIFY_BIN" | tr -d '#!')
L79:    case "$_SHEBANG" in
L80:        *[!a-zA-Z0-9/_.@-]*) ;;
L81:        *) "$_SHEBANG" -c "import graphify" 2>/dev/null && PYTHON="$_SHEBANG" ;;
L82:    esac
L83:fi
L84:# 3. Fall back to python3
L85:if [ -z "$PYTHON" ]; then PYTHON="python3"; fi
L86:if ! "$PYTHON" -c "import graphify" 2>/dev/null; then
L87:    if command -v uv >/dev/null 2>&1; then
L88:        uv tool install --upgrade graphifyy -q 2>&1 | tail -3
L89:        _UV_PY=$(uv tool run --from graphifyy python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)" 2>/dev/null)
L90:        if [ -n "$_UV_PY" ]; then PYTHON="$_UV_PY"; fi
L91:    else
L92:        "$PYTHON" -m pip install graphifyy -q 2>/dev/null \
L93:          || "$PYTHON" -m pip install graphifyy -q --break-system-packages 2>&1 | tail -3
L94:    fi
L95:fi
L96:# Write interpreter path for all subsequent steps (persists across invocations)
L97:mkdir -p graphify-out
L98:"$PYTHON" -c "import sys; open('graphify-out/.graphify_python', 'w', encoding='utf-8').write(sys.executable)"
L99:# Save scan root so `graphify update` (no args) knows where to look next time
L100:echo "$(cd INPUT_PATH && pwd)" > graphify-out/.graphify_root
L101:```
L102:
L103:If the import succeeds, print nothing and move straight to Step 2.
L104:
L105:**In every subsequent bash block, replace `python3` with `$(cat graphify-out/.graphify_python)` to use the correct interpreter.**
L106:
L107:### Step 2 - Detect files
L108:
L109:```bash
L110:$(cat graphify-out/.graphify_python) -c "
L111:import json
L112:from graphify.detect import detect
L113:from pathlib import Path
L114:result = detect(Path('INPUT_PATH'))
L115:# Write the sidecar from Python, not a shell redirect, so the same block renders
L116:# on PowerShell hosts without console-encoding drift (#2528).
L117:Path('graphify-out/.graphify_detect.json').write_text(json.dumps(result, ensure_ascii=False), encoding=\"utf-8\")
L118:print(f'Detected {result[\"total_files\"]} files')
L119:"
L120:```
L121:
L122:Replace INPUT_PATH with the actual path the user provided. Do NOT cat or print the JSON - read it silently and present a clean summary instead:
L123:
L124:```
L125:Corpus: X files · ~Y words
L126:  code:     N files (.py .ts .go ...)
L127:  docs:     N files (.md .txt ...)
L128:  papers:   N files (.pdf ...)
L129:  images:   N files
L130:  video:    N files (.mp4 .mp3 ...)
L131:```
L132:
L133:Omit any category with 0 files from the summary.
L134:
L135:Then act on it:
L136:- If `total_files` is 0: stop with "No supported files found in [path]."
L137:- If `skipped_sensitive` is non-empty: report the count and list the skipped file names, so a wrongly-flagged source or doc is visible and can be renamed or moved (#2106).
L138:- If `total_words` > 2,000,000 OR `total_files` > 500: show the warning. Then compute the top 5 first-level subdirectories by file count:
L139:  - Read `scan_root` from the detect JSON (always an absolute path to the resolved INPUT_PATH).
L140:  - Concatenate all file lists across all types (`code`, `document`, `paper`, `image`, `video`).
L141:  - Filter out any path that starts with `scan_root + "/graphify-out/"` to exclude converted sidecars.
L142:  - For each file, strip the `scan_root` prefix and take the first path component. Files directly in `scan_root` with no subdirectory count as `(root)`.
L143:  - If all files are in `(root)` with no subdirectories, do not ask to narrow — no subfolders exist. Instead suggest `--no-cluster` to skip the expensive clustering step and proceed.
L144:  - Otherwise rank by count, show the top 5 with file counts, then ask which subfolder to run on. Wait for the user's answer before proceeding.
L145:- Otherwise: proceed directly to Step 2.5 if video files were detected, or Step 3 if not.
L146:
L147:### Step 2.5 - Video and audio (only if video files detected)
L148:
L149:Skip this step entirely if `detect` returned zero `video` files. When the corpus has video or audio, see `references/transcribe.md` to transcribe them to text first, then treat the transcripts as doc files in Step 3.
L150:
L151:### Step 3 - Extract entities and relationships
L152:
L153:**Before starting:** note whether `--mode deep` was given. You must pass `DEEP_MODE=true` to every subagent in Step B2 if it was. Track this from the original invocation - do not lose it.
L154:
L155:This step has two parts: **structural extraction** (deterministic, free) and **semantic extraction** (LLM, costs tokens).
L156:
L157:> **graphify needs no API key. Never ask the user for one, and never block on one.** Code is extracted structurally (AST) with no LLM and no key at all — a code-only corpus (the common `/graphify .` on a repo) skips semantic extraction entirely, so it needs nothing here: go straight to Part A and skip Part B. Semantic extraction (only for docs, papers, and images) uses Gemini **only if** `GEMINI_API_KEY`/`GOOGLE_API_KEY` is already set; otherwise the host agent itself is the LLM. graphify does **not** read `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, or any other provider key. If you catch yourself about to prompt for, wait on, or stop because of a missing API key, that is a misread of this skill — proceed without one.
L158:
L159:**Before semantic extraction:** check whether `GEMINI_API_KEY` or `GOOGLE_API_KEY` is set. If neither is set, print this one-liner to the user:
L160:> Tip: set `GEMINI_API_KEY` or `GOOGLE_API_KEY` to use Gemini for semantic extraction (`pip install 'graphifyy[gemini]'`).
L161:
L162:Print it once, then continue — do not wait for the user to supply a key. If `GEMINI_API_KEY` or `GOOGLE_API_KEY` IS set, use `graphify.llm.extract_corpus_parallel(files, backend="gemini")` for semantic extraction instead of dispatching subagents. The default Gemini model is `gemini-3-flash-preview`; set `GRAPHIFY_GEMINI_MODEL` or pass `--model` in headless CLI flows to override it.
L163:
L164:> **No other API keys are read.** When `GEMINI_API_KEY`/`GOOGLE_API_KEY` are unset, semantic extraction falls to the host agent itself — the running session is the LLM. On a host that dispatches subagents (e.g. Claude Code), dispatch them as written in Part B. On a host that runs the CLI directly in a terminal and cannot dispatch subagents, do not stall: a code-only corpus has no semantic work, so write the empty semantic file (Part B "Fast path") and continue to Part C; for a corpus with docs/papers/images, either set a Gemini key or extract those inline yourself, but in no case prompt for `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` — that prompt is a misread of this skill.
L165:
L166:**Run Part A (AST) and Part B (semantic) in parallel. Dispatch all semantic subagents AND start AST extraction in the same message. Both can run simultaneously since they operate on different file types. Merge results in Part C as before.**
L167:
L168:Note: Parallelizing AST + semantic saves 5-15s on large corpora. AST is deterministic and fast; start it while subagents are processing docs/papers.
L169:
L170:#### Part A - Structural extraction for code files
L171:
L172:For any code files detected, run AST extraction in parallel with Part B subagents:
L173:
L174:```bash
L175:$(cat graphify-out/.graphify_python) -c "
L176:import sys, json
L177:from graphify.extract import collect_files, extract
L178:from pathlib import Path
L179:import json
L180:
L181:code_files = []
L182:detect = json.loads(Path('graphify-out/.graphify_detect.json').read_text(encoding=\"utf-8\"))
L183:for f in detect.get('files', {}).get('code', []):
L184:    code_files.extend(collect_files(Path(f)) if Path(f).is_dir() else [Path(f)])
L185:
L186:if code_files:
L187:    result = extract(code_files, cache_root=Path('INPUT_PATH'))
L188:    Path('graphify-out/.graphify_ast.json').write_text(json.dumps(result, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False), encoding=\"utf-8\")
L189:    print(f'AST: {len(result[\"nodes\"])} nodes, {len(result[\"edges\"])} edges')
L190:else:
L191:    Path('graphify-out/.graphify_ast.json').write_text(json.dumps({'nodes':[],'edges':[],'input_tokens':0,'output_tokens':0}, ensure_ascii=False), encoding=\"utf-8\")
L192:    print('No code files - skipping AST extraction')
L193:"
L194:```
L195:
L196:#### Part B - Semantic extraction (parallel subagents)
L197:
L198:**Fast path:** If detection found zero docs, papers, and images (code-only corpus), skip Part B entirely and go straight to Part C. AST handles code - there is nothing for semantic subagents to do. **First write an empty semantic file** so Part C's merge has its input (it reads `.graphify_semantic.json` unconditionally; without this a code-only run hits `FileNotFoundError`):
L199:
L200:```bash
L201:$(cat graphify-out/.graphify_python) -c "
L202:import json
L203:from pathlib import Path
L204:Path('graphify-out/.graphify_semantic.json').write_text(json.dumps({'nodes':[],'edges':[],'hyperedges':[],'input_tokens':0,'output_tokens':0}), encoding='utf-8')
L205:"
L206:```
L207:
L208:**MANDATORY: You MUST use the Agent tool here. Reading files yourself one-by-one is forbidden - it is 5-10x slower. If you do not use the Agent tool you are doing this wrong.**
L209:
L210:Before dispatching subagents, print a timing estimate:
L211:- Load `total_words` and file counts from `graphify-out/.graphify_detect.json`
L212:- Estimate agents needed: `ceil(uncached_non_code_files / 22)` (chunk size is 20-25)
L213:- Estimate time: ~45s per agent batch (they run in parallel, so total ≈ 45s × ceil(agents/parallel_limit))
L214:- Print: "Semantic extraction: ~N files → X agents, estimated ~Ys"
L215:
L216:**Step B0 - Check extraction cache first**
L217:
L218:Before dispatching any subagents, check which files already have cached extraction results:
L219:
L220:SPEC_PATH below is the **absolute** path of the `references/extraction-spec.md` that ships beside this SKILL.md — the same file Step B2 loads and hands to every subagent. It is the extraction prompt, so cache entries are attributed to it: when a graphify upgrade changes the prompt, entries produced by the old one are re-extracted instead of replayed, and unchanged prompts keep their entries (#1939). Substitute the real path in both Step B0 and Step B3 — pass the same one to each, and do not drop the argument.
L221:
L222:```bash
L223:$(cat graphify-out/.graphify_python) -c "
L224:import json
L225:from graphify.cache import check_semantic_cache
L226:from pathlib import Path
L227:
L228:detect = json.loads(Path('graphify-out/.graphify_detect.json').read_text(encoding=\"utf-8\"))
L229:# Only content files go to semantic extraction. Code is already covered structurally
L230:# by the AST pass (Part A); flattening every category here makes subagents re-read
L231:# every source file (#1392). Video is transcribed to a document in Step 2.5 first.
L232:all_files = [f for cat in ('document', 'paper', 'image') for f in detect['files'].get(cat, [])]
L233:
L234:cached_nodes, cached_edges, cached_hyperedges, uncached = check_semantic_cache(all_files, root='INPUT_PATH', prompt_file='SPEC_PATH')
L235:
L236:# Always (re)write the cache file: write hits, else DELETE any leftover from a prior
L237:# run so Part C never merges a stale .graphify_cached.json (#1392).
L238:if cached_nodes or cached_edges or cached_hyperedges:
L239:    Path('graphify-out/.graphify_cached.json').write_text(json.dumps({'nodes': cached_nodes, 'edges': cached_edges, 'hyperedges': cached_hyperedges}, ensure_ascii=False), encoding=\"utf-8\")
L240:else:
L241:    Path('graphify-out/.graphify_cached.json').unlink(missing_ok=True)
L242:Path('graphify-out/.graphify_uncached.txt').write_text('\n'.join(uncached), encoding=\"utf-8\")
L243:print(f'Cache: {len(all_files)-len(uncached)} files hit, {len(uncached)} files need extraction')
L244:"
L245:```
L246:
L247:Only dispatch subagents for files listed in `graphify-out/.graphify_uncached.txt`. If all files are cached, skip to Part C directly.
L248:
L249:**Step B1 - Split into chunks**
L250:
L251:Load files from `graphify-out/.graphify_uncached.txt`. Split into chunks of 20-25 files each. Each image gets its own chunk (vision needs separate context). When splitting, group files from the same directory together so related artifacts land in the same chunk and cross-file relationships are more likely to be extracted.
L252:
L253:**Step B2 - Dispatch ALL subagents in a single message**
L254:
L255:Call the Agent tool multiple times IN THE SAME RESPONSE - one call per chunk. This is the only way they run in parallel. If you make one Agent call, wait, then make another, you are doing it sequentially and defeating the purpose.
L256:
L257:**IMPORTANT - subagent type:** Always use `subagent_type="general-purpose"`. Do NOT use `Explore` - it is read-only and cannot write chunk files to disk, which silently drops extraction results. General-purpose has Write and Bash access which the subagent needs.
L258:
L259:Concrete example for 3 chunks:
L260:```
L261:[Agent tool call 1: files 1-15, subagent_type="general-purpose"]
L262:[Agent tool call 2: files 16-30, subagent_type="general-purpose"]
L263:[Agent tool call 3: files 31-45, subagent_type="general-purpose"]
L264:```
L265:All three in one message. Not three separate messages.
L266:
L267:Each subagent receives this exact prompt (substitute FILE_LIST, CHUNK_NUM, TOTAL_CHUNKS, DEEP_MODE, and CHUNK_PATH).
L268:
L269:CHUNK_PATH must be an **absolute** path — derive it before dispatching:
L270:```bash
L271:PROJECT_ROOT=$(pwd)  # cwd — where Part C globs graphify-out/ (NOT .graphify_root/scan dir, #1392)
L272:# Then for chunk N: CHUNK_PATH="${PROJECT_ROOT}/graphify-out/.graphify_chunk_0N.json"
L273:```
L274:
L275:Subagent prompt template:
L276:
L277:See `references/extraction-spec.md` for the exact subagent prompt (JSON schema, node-ID rules, confidence rubric, frontmatter, hyperedge, and vision rules). Load it only here, only when at least one chunk holds a doc, paper, or image; a pure-code corpus has skipped Part B and never reads it. Pass each subagent that prompt verbatim with FILE_LIST, CHUNK_NUM, TOTAL_CHUNKS, DEEP_MODE, and CHUNK_PATH substituted, and have it write the result to CHUNK_PATH.
L278:
L279:**Step B3 - Collect, cache, and merge**
L280:
L281:Wait for all subagents. For each result:
L282:- Check that `graphify-out/.graphify_chunk_NN.json` exists on disk — this is the success signal
L283:- If the file exists and contains valid JSON with `nodes` and `edges`, include it and save to cache
L284:- If the file is missing, the subagent was likely dispatched as read-only (Explore type) — print a warning: "chunk N missing from disk — subagent may have been read-only. Re-run with general-purpose agent." Do not silently skip.
L285:- If a subagent failed or returned invalid JSON, print a warning and skip that chunk - do not abort
L286:
L287:If more than half the chunks failed or are missing, stop and tell the user to re-run and ensure `subagent_type="general-purpose"` is used.
L288:
L289:Merge all chunk files into `.graphify_semantic_new.json`. **After each Agent call completes, read the real token counts from the Agent tool result's `usage` field and write them back into the chunk JSON before merging** — the chunk JSON itself always has placeholder zeros. Then run:
L290:```bash
L291:$(cat graphify-out/.graphify_python) -c "
L292:import json, glob
L293:from pathlib import Path
L294:
L295:chunks = sorted(glob.glob('graphify-out/.graphify_chunk_*.json'))
L296:all_nodes, all_edges, all_hyperedges = [], [], []
L297:total_in, total_out = 0, 0
L298:for c in chunks:
L299:    d = json.loads(Path(c).read_text(encoding=\"utf-8\"))
L300:    all_nodes += d.get('nodes', [])
L301:    all_edges += d.get('edges', [])
L302:    all_hyperedges += d.get('hyperedges', [])
L303:    total_in += d.get('input_tokens', 0)
L304:    total_out += d.get('output_tokens', 0)
L305:Path('graphify-out/.graphify_semantic_new.json').write_text(json.dumps({
L306:    'nodes': all_nodes, 'edges': all_edges, 'hyperedges': all_hyperedges,
L307:    'input_tokens': total_in, 'output_tokens': total_out,
L308:}, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False), encoding=\"utf-8\")
L309:print(f'Merged {len(chunks)} chunks: {total_in:,} in / {total_out:,} out tokens')
L310:"
L311:```
L312:
L313:Save new results to cache. Pass the same SPEC_PATH as Step B0 — it stamps each entry with the prompt that produced it, and a write under a different prompt than the read lands where the next run won't look (#1939):
L314:```bash
L315:$(cat graphify-out/.graphify_python) -c "
L316:import json
L317:from graphify.cache import save_semantic_cache
L318:from pathlib import Path
L319:
L320:new = json.loads(Path('graphify-out/.graphify_semantic_new.json').read_text(encoding=\"utf-8\")) if Path('graphify-out/.graphify_semantic_new.json').exists() else {'nodes':[],'edges':[],'hyperedges':[]}
L321:uncached = [line for line in Path('graphify-out/.graphify_uncached.txt').read_text(encoding=\"utf-8\").splitlines() if line]
L322:saved = save_semantic_cache(new.get('nodes', []), new.get('edges', []), new.get('hyperedges', []), root='INPUT_PATH', allowed_source_files=uncached, prompt_file='SPEC_PATH')
L323:print(f'Cached {saved} files')
L324:"
L325:```
L326:
L327:Merge cached + new results into `graphify-out/.graphify_semantic.json`:
L328:```bash
L329:$(cat graphify-out/.graphify_python) -c "
L330:import json
L331:from pathlib import Path
L332:
L333:cached = json.loads(Path('graphify-out/.graphify_cached.json').read_text(encoding=\"utf-8\")) if Path('graphify-out/.graphify_cached.json').exists() else {'nodes':[],'edges':[],'hyperedges':[]}

L393:### Step 4 - Build graph, cluster, analyze, generate outputs
L394:
L395:**Before starting:** the code blocks below pass `directed=IS_DIRECTED` to `build_from_json()`. Replace `IS_DIRECTED` with `True` if `--directed` was given (builds a `DiGraph` preserving edge direction source→target), otherwise `False` (the default undirected `Graph`). Substitute it the same way you substitute `INPUT_PATH` — do not leave the literal `IS_DIRECTED` in the code.

L397:```bash
L398:mkdir -p graphify-out
L399:$(cat graphify-out/.graphify_python) -c "
L400:import sys, json
L401:from graphify.build import build_from_json
L402:from graphify.cluster import cluster, score_all
L403:from graphify.analyze import god_nodes, surprising_connections, suggest_questions
L404:from graphify.report import generate
L405:from graphify.export import to_json
L406:from pathlib import Path

L412:# base so the full build and incremental --update never drift apart on re-extract.

L423:gods = god_nodes(G)

L440:analysis = {

L442:    'cohesion': {str(k): v for k, v in cohesion.items()},
L443:    'gods': gods,
L444:    'surprises': surprises,
L445:    'questions': questions,
L446:}
L447:Path('graphify-out/.graphify_analysis.json').write_text(json.dumps(analysis, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False), encoding=\"utf-8\")
L448:print(f'Graph: {G.number_of_nodes()} nodes, {G.number_of_edges()} edges, {len(communities)} communities')

L456:### Step 4.5 - Graph health check (read-only integrity gate)
L457:
L458:A non-destructive diagnostic on the extraction, before labeling. It surfaces edge collapse, dangling/missing endpoints, and self-loops — the silent-corruption modes of incremental updates and AST/LLM id mismatches. Read-only; never aborts.
L459:
L460:```bash
L461:$(cat graphify-out/.graphify_python) -c "
L462:import json
L463:from pathlib import Path
L464:from graphify.diagnostics import diagnose_extraction, format_diagnostic_report
L465:
L466:extraction = json.loads(Path('graphify-out/.graphify_extract.json').read_text(encoding=\"utf-8\"))
L467:summary = diagnose_extraction(extraction, directed=IS_DIRECTED, root='INPUT_PATH')
L468:print(format_diagnostic_report(summary))
L469:flags = [f'{summary[k]} {label}' for k, label in (
L470:    ('dangling_endpoint_edges', 'dangling-endpoint edges'),
L471:    ('missing_endpoint_edges', 'missing-endpoint edges'),
L472:    ('self_loop_edges', 'self-loop edges'),
L473:    ('directed_same_endpoint_collapsed_edges', 'collapsed (directed) edges'),
L474:    ('undirected_same_endpoint_collapsed_edges', 'collapsed (undirected) edges'),
L475:) if summary.get(k, 0)]
L476:print('GRAPH HEALTH WARNING: ' + '; '.join(flags) + ' - graph may be incomplete/corrupt.' if flags else 'Graph health: OK (no dangling/missing/collapsed edges).')
L477:"
L478:```
L479:
L480:Substitute `IS_DIRECTED` and `INPUT_PATH` as in Step 4. If a `GRAPH HEALTH WARNING` prints, surface it in the final summary (do not abort — the graph is still usable, but the integrity issue must be visible, per the Honesty Rules).

L556:
L557:### Step 9 - Save manifest, update cost tracker, clean up, and report
L558:
L559:```bash
L560:$(cat graphify-out/.graphify_python) -c "
L561:import json
L562:from pathlib import Path
L563:from datetime import datetime, timezone
L564:from graphify.detect import save_manifest
L565:
L566:# Save manifest for --update
L567:detect = json.loads(Path('graphify-out/.graphify_detect.json').read_text(encoding=\"utf-8\"))
L568:extract = json.loads(Path('graphify-out/.graphify_extract.json').read_text(encoding=\"utf-8\"))
L569:# In --update mode, 'all_files' carries the full corpus; 'files' is the changed
L570:# subset. Full-rebuild mode populates only 'files', so the fallback handles that.
L571:# root= relativizes the manifest keys to the scan root (same base as the build),
L572:# so the on-disk manifest is portable across clones/machines and a later --update
L573:# matches cached files instead of missing every one (#1417).
L574:#
L575:# Only stamp semantic files (docs/papers/images) that ACTUALLY produced output:
L576:# a detected file whose chunk failed or was omitted must stay unstamped so the
L577:# next --update re-queues it, otherwise it is marked done and its content is lost
L578:# forever (#2015). This mirrors the library extract path exactly
L579:# (cli._stamped_manifest_files + clear_semantic + scan_corpus); do not stamp the
L580:# raw corpus. Code files are always stamped (AST is deterministic); only semantic
L581:# types are gated on output.
L582:from graphify.cli import _stamped_manifest_files
L583:_corpus = detect.get('all_files') or detect['files']
L584:_manifest_files = _stamped_manifest_files(_corpus, extract, Path('INPUT_PATH'))
L585:# Files dispatched this run (the changed subset) but NOT stamped above still carry
L586:# a stale semantic_hash from a prior run; clear it so detect_incremental re-queues
L587:# them instead of reading them as unchanged (#1948).
L588:_sem_types = ('document', 'paper', 'image')
L589:_dispatched = {f for t, fl in detect['files'].items() if t in _sem_types for f in fl}
L590:_stamped = {f for fl in _manifest_files.values() for f in fl}
L591:_cleared = _dispatched - _stamped
L592:# scan_corpus = the RAW full corpus (not the stamp-filtered subset) so in-root
L593:# files newly excluded since last run are dropped rather than masquerading as
L594:# deletions; untouched files' prior rows are still preserved (#1908).
L595:_scan = {f for fl in _corpus.values() for f in fl}
L596:save_manifest(_manifest_files, root='INPUT_PATH', scan_corpus=_scan, clear_semantic=_cleared or None)
L597:
L598:# Update cumulative cost tracker
L599:input_tok = extract.get('input_tokens', 0)
L600:output_tok = extract.get('output_tokens', 0)
L601:
L602:cost_path = Path('graphify-out/cost.json')
L603:if cost_path.exists():
L604:    cost = json.loads(cost_path.read_text(encoding=\"utf-8\"))
L605:else:
L606:    cost = {'runs': [], 'total_input_tokens': 0, 'total_output_tokens': 0}
L607:
L608:cost['runs'].append({
L609:    'date': datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
L610:    'input_tokens': input_tok,
L611:    'output_tokens': output_tok,
L612:    'files': detect.get('total_files', 0),
L613:})
L614:cost['total_input_tokens'] += input_tok
L615:cost['total_output_tokens'] += output_tok
L616:cost_path.write_text(json.dumps(cost, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False), encoding=\"utf-8\")
L617:
L618:print(f'This run: {input_tok:,} input tokens, {output_tok:,} output tokens')
L619:print(f'All time: {cost[\"total_input_tokens\"]:,} input, {cost[\"total_output_tokens\"]:,} output ({len(cost[\"runs\"])} runs)')
L620:"
L621:rm -f graphify-out/.graphify_detect.json graphify-out/.graphify_extract.json graphify-out/.graphify_ast.json graphify-out/.graphify_semantic.json graphify-out/.graphify_analysis.json
L622:find graphify-out -maxdepth 1 -name '.graphify_chunk_*.json' -delete 2>/dev/null
L623:rm -f graphify-out/.needs_update 2>/dev/null || true
L624:```
L625:
L626:Replace INPUT_PATH with the actual path (same value used in Steps 4-5) so the manifest is relativized to the scan root.
L627:
L628:Tell the user (omit the obsidian line unless --obsidian was given):
L629:```
L630:Graph complete. Outputs in PATH_TO_DIR/graphify-out/
L631:
L632:  graph.html            - interactive graph, open in browser
L633:  GRAPH_REPORT.md       - audit report
L634:  graph.json            - raw graph data
L635:  obsidian/             - Obsidian vault (only if --obsidian was given)
L636:```
L637:
L638:If graphify saved you time, consider supporting it: https://github.com/sponsors/safishamsi
L639:
L640:Replace PATH_TO_DIR with the actual absolute path of the directory that was processed.
L641:
L642:Then paste these sections from GRAPH_REPORT.md directly into the chat:
L643:- God Nodes
L644:- Surprising Connections
L645:- Suggested Questions
L646:
L647:Do NOT paste the full report - just those three sections. Keep it concise.
L648:
L649:Then immediately offer to explore. Pick the single most interesting suggested question from the report - the one that crosses the most community boundaries or has the most surprising bridge node - and ask:
L650:
L651:> "The most interesting question this graph can answer: **[question]**. Want me to trace it?"
L652:
L653:If the user says yes, run `/graphify query "[question]"` on the graph and walk them through the answer using the graph structure - which nodes connect, which community boundaries get crossed, what the path reveals. Keep going as long as they want to explore. Each answer should end with a natural follow-up ("this connects to X - want to go deeper?") so the session feels like navigation, not a one-shot report.
L654:
L655:The graph is the map. Your job after the pipeline is to be the guide.
L656:
L657:---
L658:
L659:## Interpreter guard for subcommands
L660:
L661:Before running any subcommand below (`--update`, `--cluster-only`, `query`, `path`, `explain`, `add`), check that `.graphify_python` exists. If it's missing (e.g. user deleted `graphify-out/`), re-resolve the interpreter first:
L662:
L663:```bash
L664:if [ ! -f graphify-out/.graphify_python ]; then
L665:    GRAPHIFY_BIN=$(which graphify 2>/dev/null)
L666:    if [ -n "$GRAPHIFY_BIN" ]; then
L667:        PYTHON=$(head -1 "$GRAPHIFY_BIN" | tr -d '#!')
L668:        case "$PYTHON" in *[!a-zA-Z0-9/_.@-]*) PYTHON="python3" ;; esac
L669:    else
L670:        PYTHON="python3"
L671:    fi
L672:    mkdir -p graphify-out
L673:    "$PYTHON" -c "import sys; open('graphify-out/.graphify_python', 'w', encoding='utf-8').write(sys.executable)"
L674:fi
L675:```
L676:
L677:## For --update and --cluster-only
L678:
L679:Both are non-default subcommands. `--update` re-extracts only new or changed files; `--cluster-only` reruns clustering on the existing graph. See `references/update.md` for both flows.
L680:
L681:---
L682:
L683:## For /graphify query
L684:
L685:When `graphify-out/graph.json` already exists and the user asks a question about the corpus, answer from the graph rather than rebuilding it:
L686:
L687:```bash
L688:graphify query "<question>"
L689:```
L690:
L691:Before traversal, expand the question against the graph's own vocabulary so a wording mismatch does not collapse the answer to noise. If the `graphify query` CLI is unavailable, fall back to an inline NetworkX traversal of `graphify-out/graph.json`. Answer using only what the graph output contains, and quote `source_location` when citing a specific fact. For that vocab-expansion step, the BFS/DFS traversal modes, the `--budget` cap, the NetworkX fallback, `save-result` feedback, and the `/graphify path` and `/graphify explain` flows, see `references/query.md`.
L692:
L693:---
L694:
L695:## For /graphify add and --watch
L696:
L697:Neither is part of the default build. When the user runs `/graphify add <url>` to fetch a URL into the corpus, or passes `--watch` to auto-rebuild on file changes, see `references/add-watch.md`.
L698:
L699:---
L700:
L701:## For the commit hook and native CLAUDE.md integration
L702:
L703:When the user asks to install the post-commit auto-rebuild hook or wire graphify into a project's CLAUDE.md, see `references/hooks.md`.
L704:
L705:---
L706:
L707:## Honesty Rules
L708:
L709:- Never invent an edge. If unsure, use AMBIGUOUS.
L710:- Never skip the corpus check warning.
L711:- Always show token cost in the report.
L712:- Never hide cohesion scores behind symbols - show the raw number.
L713:- Never run HTML viz on a graph with more than 5,000 nodes without warning the user.
L714:

L1:# UI Flow Specification
L2:
L3:## 1. Overview
L4:
L5:This document defines the user interface flow for the Support Ticket Management System. The interface is designed for a simple, clear support workflow with ticket creation, listing, viewing, updating, status changes, comments, search, and status-based filtering.
L6:
L7:The UI should remain straightforward and user-friendly, with clear feedback for loading, empty states, validation, and API failure scenarios.
L8:
L9:## 2. Screen: Ticket List
L10:
L11:### 2.1 Purpose
L12:
L13:The Ticket List screen is the primary landing view for users. It shows all tickets and enables users to search, filter, create a new ticket, and open a ticket for more detail.
L14:
L15:### 2.2 Layout
L16:
L17:- Header or page title: "Tickets"
L18:- Search input for keyword search
L19:- Status filter dropdown or segmented control
L20:- Create Ticket button
L21:- Ticket table or list view with summary rows
L22:
L23:### 2.3 Ticket list item content
L24:
L25:Each ticket row should display:
L26:
L27:- ticket identifier
L28:- title
L29:- current status
L30:- priority
L31:- assignee, if available
L32:- last updated time or creation time
L33:
L34:### 2.4 User actions
L35:
L36:- Search by keyword
L37:- Filter by status
L38:- Open a ticket to view details
L39:- Create a new ticket
L40:
L41:### 2.5 Pagination
L42:
L43:- If the ticket list API uses pagination, the UI should provide controls to navigate between result pages.
L44:- The UI should display the current page and available navigation options.
L45:- The UI should preserve the active search and status filter when changing pages.
L46:- Pagination controls should be disabled while the corresponding request is loading.
L47:### 2.6 Loading state
L48:
L49:- Show a spinner, skeleton rows, or loading text while tickets are being fetched.
L50:- Disable related controls while the list is loading if needed.
L51:
L52:### 2.7 Empty state
L53:
L54:- If no tickets exist, show a friendly empty state such as:
L55:  - "No tickets found"
L56:  - "Create a new ticket to get started"
L57:- If a search or filter returns no results, show a related empty state such as:
L58:  - "No tickets match your search"
L59:  - "No tickets found for the selected status"
L60:
L61:### 2.8 Validation and API errors
L62:
L63:- If the search request fails, show a non-blocking error message.
L64:- If the ticket list request fails, show a clear error banner or inline message.
L65:- Do not display technical backend details to the end user.
L66:
L67:## 3. Flow: Create Ticket
L68:
L69:### 3.1 Trigger
L70:
L71:Triggered from the Ticket List screen via the "Create Ticket" button.
L72:
L73:### 3.2 Form fields
L74:
L75:- Title
L76:- Description
L77:- Priority
L78:- Assignee (optional depending on workflow design)
L79:
L80:### 3.3 Validation
L81:
L82:- Title is required.
L83:- Description is required.
L84:- Priority must be a valid supported value.
L85:- Assignee, if included, must be valid when provided.
L86:
L87:### 3.4 Error handling
L88:
L89:- Display inline validation errors next to invalid fields.
L90:- Show a top-level form error if the backend rejects the create request.
L91:- Do not leave the user guessing; show a clear message such as "Unable to create ticket. Please check the details and try again."
L92:
L93:### 3.5 Success behaviour
L94:
L95:- On successful creation, the user is returned to the Ticket List screen.
L96:- The UI must refresh or re-fetch the ticket list after successful creation.
L97:- The newly created ticket should be available in the refreshed list.
L98:- The created ticket must have an initial status of `OPEN`.
L99:
L100:### 3.6 Loading state
L101:
L102:- Disable the submit button while creation is in progress.
L103:- Show a loading state such as "Creating ticket...".
L104:
L105:## 4. Screen: Ticket Details
L106:
L107:### 4.1 Purpose
L108:
L109:The Ticket Details screen shows the complete information for a selected ticket and provides actions to update the ticket, change status, and add comments.
L110:
L111:### 4.2 Content
L112:
L113:- Ticket title
L114:- Ticket description
L115:- Current status
L116:- Priority
L117:- Assignee
L118:- Creation timestamp
L119:- Updated timestamp
L120:- Comments list
L121:
L122:### 4.3 User actions
L123:
L124:- Edit Ticket
L125:- Change Status
L126:- Add Comment
L127:- Return to the Ticket List
L128:
L129:### 4.4 Loading state
L130:
L131:- Display a spinner or loading placeholder while the ticket detail is being fetched.
L132:- If the ticket cannot be loaded, show a clear error state.
L133:
L134:### 4.5 Error state
L135:
L136:- If the selected ticket is not found, show a not-found state with a message such as "Ticket not found" and a way to return to the list.
L137:- If the fetch fails, show a meaningful error message and a retry option when appropriate.
L138:
L139:## 5. Flow: Edit Ticket
L140:
L141:### 5.1 Trigger
L142:
L143:Triggered from the Ticket Details screen through an "Edit Ticket" action.
L144:
L145:### 5.2 Form fields
L146:
L147:- Title
L148:- Description
L149:- Priority
L150:- Assignee
L151:
L152:The UI must respect the ticket's current lifecycle state when determining whether ticket fields can be edited.
L153:
L154:Unless the business rules explicitly allow editing terminal tickets, tickets in `CLOSED` or `CANCELLED` state should be treated as read-only.
L155:
L156:### 5.3 Validation
L157:
L158:- Title must not be blank.
L159:- Description must not be blank.
L160:- Priority must be valid.
L161:- Assignee must be valid when provided.
L162:
L163:### 5.4 Loading state
L164:
L165:- Show a loading indicator while the update request is in progress.
L166:- Disable form submission while saving.
L167:
L168:### 5.5 Validation errors
L169:
L170:- Show inline errors next to invalid form fields.
L171:- Show a general form-level error if the backend rejects the update.
L172:
L173:### 5.6 API errors
L174:
L175:- Show a clear error alert if the update request fails.
L176:- Preserve the form values if possible so the user can correct them.
L177:
L178:### 5.7 Success behaviour
L179:
L180:- Save the updated values.
L181:- Return to the Ticket Details screen with the updated data.
L182:
L183:## 6. Flow: Change Status
L184:
L185:### 6.1 Trigger
L186:
L187:Triggered from the Ticket Details screen through a status action or status selector.
L188:
L189:### 6.2 Status model
L190:
L191:Valid states:
L192:
L193:- OPEN
L194:- IN_PROGRESS
L195:- RESOLVED
L196:- CLOSED
L197:- CANCELLED
L198:
L199:### 6.3 Allowed transitions
L200:
L201:- OPEN -> IN_PROGRESS
L202:- IN_PROGRESS -> RESOLVED
L203:- RESOLVED -> CLOSED
L204:- OPEN -> CANCELLED
L205:- IN_PROGRESS -> CANCELLED
L206:
L207:### 6.4 Status transition actions
L208:
L209:- The UI should display only the status actions that are valid for the ticket's current state.
L210:- The UI may prevent users from selecting invalid transitions.
L211:- The backend remains the authoritative source for transition validation.
L212:- The UI must handle a `409 Conflict` response if the backend rejects a transition.
L213:
L214:Valid actions:
L215:
L216:- `OPEN` -> `IN_PROGRESS`
L217:- `OPEN` -> `CANCELLED`
L218:- `IN_PROGRESS` -> `RESOLVED`
L219:- `IN_PROGRESS` -> `CANCELLED`
L220:- `RESOLVED` -> `CLOSED`
L221:
L222:No status-change action should be offered for `CLOSED` or `CANCELLED`.
L223:
L224:### 6.5 Confirmation for terminal transitions
L225:
L226:- The UI should request confirmation before performing a transition that moves the ticket into a terminal state.
L227:- Confirmation should be required for:
L228:  - `OPEN -> CANCELLED`
L229:  - `IN_PROGRESS -> CANCELLED`
L230:  - `RESOLVED -> CLOSED`
L231:- The confirmation message should clearly identify that the action changes the ticket to a terminal state.
L232:- Cancelling the confirmation must leave the ticket unchanged.
L233:- The backend must still validate the transition after confirmation.
L234:
L235:### 6.6 Status display
L236:
L237:- Display the current ticket status clearly and consistently.
L238:- Use a badge, pill, or label with distinct colors or styling for each status.
L239:- Show status in a way that helps users quickly understand the ticket lifecycle.
L240:
L241:### 6.7 Validation and API errors
L242:
L243:- If the user attempts an invalid transition, show a clear message such as:
L244:  - "This status change is not allowed for the current ticket state."
L245:- If the backend rejects the status update, surface an API error message without exposing internal details.
L246:
L247:### 6.8 Loading state
L248:
L249:- Show a loading indicator or disabled state during status submission.
L250:
L251:### 6.9 Terminal-state behaviour
L252:
L253:- `CLOSED` and `CANCELLED` are terminal states.
L254:- A ticket in `CLOSED` state must not provide an action to reopen or change its status.
L255:- A ticket in `CANCELLED` state must not provide an action to reopen or change its status.
L256:- The UI may present terminal tickets as read-only with respect to status changes.
L257:- The backend remains authoritative and must reject invalid transitions even if the UI does not expose those actions.
L258:
L259:## 7. Flow: Add Comment
L260:
L261:### 7.1 Trigger
L262:
L263:Triggered from the Ticket Details screen through an "Add Comment" action or comment form.
L264:
L265:### 7.2 Form fields
L266:
L267:- Comment text
L268:
L269:### 7.3 Validation
L270:
L271:- Comment content is required.
L272:- Comment content must not be empty or whitespace-only.
L273:- The ticket must exist.
L274:- Whether comments are allowed on `CLOSED` or `CANCELLED` tickets must follow the application's business rule.
L275:- If comments are not allowed on terminal tickets, the UI must disable the comment form for `CLOSED` and `CANCELLED` tickets.
L276:- The backend must remain authoritative for this rule.
L277:
L278:### 7.4 Loading state
L279:
L280:- Disable the submit action while the comment is being posted.
L281:- Show a loading indicator such as "Adding comment..."
L282:
L283:### 7.5 Validation errors
L284:
L285:- Show inline validation for an empty or invalid comment.
L286:
L287:### 7.6 API errors
L288:
L289:- Show a generic error such as "Unable to add comment. Please try again."
L290:- Keep the form present so the user can correct the input.
L291:
L292:### 7.7 Success behaviour
L293:
L294:- Append the new comment to the comments list.
L295:- Preserve ticket detail view context after success.
L296:
L297:## 8. Search
L298:
L299:### 8.1 Purpose
L300:
L301:Search allows users to find tickets by keyword.
L302:
L303:### 8.2 Controls
L304:
L305:- Search input in the Ticket List header
L306:- Search trigger by button or on input depending on UX design
L307:
L308:### 8.3 Behaviour
L309:
L310:- Search matches ticket title and description according to the backend API contract.
L311:- When the search field contains a valid keyword, the UI calls the search API.
L312:- When the search field is blank, the UI uses the normal ticket-list API without a keyword.
L313:- The UI must not send an empty keyword to an endpoint that requires a non-empty keyword.
L314:- If the backend returns no matches, show an appropriate empty state.
L315:
L316:### 8.4 Validation and errors
L317:
L318:- Empty search values should be treated as a normal list request or ignored gracefully.
L319:- Display a clear error message if the search request fails.
L320:
L321:## 9. Status filtering
L322:
L323:### 9.1 Purpose
L324:
L325:Users can filter tickets by current status.
L326:
L327:### 9.2 Controls
L328:
L329:- Status dropdown or filter buttons for each valid status.
L330:
L331:### 9.3 Supported values
L332:
L333:Ticket status values:
L334:
L335:- `OPEN`
L336:- `IN_PROGRESS`
L337:- `RESOLVED`
L338:- `CLOSED`
L339:- `CANCELLED`
L340:
L341:The UI should also provide an `All statuses` option.
L342:
L343:`All statuses` means that no `status` query parameter is sent to the backend.
L344:
L345:### 9.4 Behaviour
L346:
L347:- Filtering should display only tickets matching the selected status.
L348:- If no tickets match, show a filtered empty state.
L349:
L350:### 9.5 Validation and errors
L351:
L352:- If the filter value is invalid, show a clear error and reset to the default state if appropriate.
L353:- If the backend returns an error, show a non-blocking message.
L354:
L355:## 10. Status display conventions
L356:
L357:The UI should present statuses in a consistent and clear manner.
L358:
L359:- OPEN: neutral or open state styling
L360:- IN_PROGRESS: active/in-progress styling
L361:- RESOLVED: successful or complete styling
L362:- CLOSED: final or closed styling
L363:- CANCELLED: cancelled/secondary styling
L364:
L365:Use a consistent badge, label, or color scheme throughout the app.
L366:
L367:## 11. Validation error patterns
L368:
L369:Validation errors should be shown in a consistent way across screens:
L370:
L371:- Inline text under the relevant field
L372:- Form-level summary for multiple errors
L373:- Clear and actionable wording
L374:
L375:Examples:
L376:
L377:- "Title is required."
L378:- "Description cannot be blank."
L379:- "Please select a valid status."
L380:- "This status change is not allowed for the current ticket state."
L381:
L382:## 12. API error patterns
L383:
L384:API failures should be presented in a user-friendly way:
L385:
L386:- For network or server errors: show a generic alert such as "Unable to load tickets. Please try again."
L387:- For not-found errors: show a not-found state for the ticket or redirect to the list if appropriate.
L388:- For invalid state transitions: show a business-rule message that explains the user cannot make that status change.
L389:
L390:## 13. API error mapping
L391:
L392:The UI should map API responses to user-friendly messages without exposing internal implementation details.
L393:
L394:| HTTP status | UI behaviour |
L395:| --- | --- |
L396:| `400 Bad Request` | Display validation or invalid-request feedback |
L397:| `404 Not Found` | Display a not-found state for the requested ticket |
L398:| `409 Conflict` | Display the business-rule error, especially for invalid status transitions |
L399:| `422 Unprocessable Entity` | Display business validation feedback when used by the API |
L400:| `500 Internal Server Error` | Display a generic server-error message |
L401:| Network failure | Display a retryable connection/error message |
L402:
L403:Field-level validation errors should be displayed next to the relevant fields when the API provides field information.
L404:
L405:## 14. Accessibility and clarity
L406:
L407:- Ensure all actions and error messages are readable and accessible.
L408:- Use labels, visible focus states, and clear call-to-action wording.
L409:- Keep the UI simple and consistent across screens.
L410:
L411:## 15. Scope note
L412:
L413:This document defines the user flows and interface behavior for the Support Ticket Management System. It specifies the primary screens, states, validation expectations, feedback patterns, and status-management behavior, without prescribing implementation code.
L414:

L1:# Requirements Specification
L2:
L3:## 1. Project Objective
L4:
L5:The project objective is to build a Support Ticket Management System that enables users to create, view, search, filter, update, and manage support tickets throughout their lifecycle. The system must persist ticket data in a database, validate input on the backend, and provide clear error messages in the user interface.
L6:
L7:## 2. Actors
L8:
L9:- AA-001: Support user — a user who creates, views, searches, filters, and updates tickets.
L10:- AA-002: Assignee — a user assigned to a ticket who can receive updates and participate in ticket resolution.
L11:- AA-003: System — the application platform responsible for persistence, validation, business rules, and error handling.
L12:
L13:## 3. Functional Requirements
L14:
L15:- FR-001: The system shall allow a support user to create a new ticket.
L16:- FR-002: The system shall allow a support user to list all tickets.
L17:- FR-003: The system shall allow a support user to view the details of a specific ticket.
L18:- FR-004: The system shall allow a support user to update a ticket title.
L19:- FR-005: The system shall allow a support user to update a ticket description.
L20:- FR-006: The system shall allow a support user to update a ticket priority.
L21:- FR-007: The system shall allow a support user to update the assignee for a ticket.
L22:- FR-008: The system shall allow a support user to add comments to a ticket.
L23:- FR-009: The system shall allow a support user to search tickets by keyword.
L24:- FR-010: The system shall allow a support user to filter tickets by status.
L25:- FR-011: The system shall persist ticket data and ticket comments in a database.
L26:- FR-012: The system shall provide a user-visible way to view meaningful error messages when an operation fails or input is invalid.
L27:- FR-013: The system shall preserve persisted ticket and comment data across application restarts.
L28:- FR-014: The system shall enforce the following and only the following valid ticket status transitions:
L29:  - OPEN → IN_PROGRESS
L30:  - IN_PROGRESS → RESOLVED
L31:  - RESOLVED → CLOSED
L32:  - OPEN → CANCELLED
L33:  - IN_PROGRESS → CANCELLED
L34:- FR-015: The backend shall reject any status transition not defined in FR-014.
L35:- FR-016: The system shall reject transitions such as CLOSED → OPEN, RESOLVED → OPEN, and CANCELLED → OPEN as invalid state changes.
L36:
L37:## 4. Non-Functional Requirements
L38:
L39:- NFR-001: The system shall validate all incoming data on the backend before persisting or processing it.
L40:- NFR-002: The system shall provide clear and meaningful user-facing error messages for invalid input and failed operations.
L41:- NFR-003: The system shall store ticket data in a persistent database.
L42:- NFR-004: The system shall support basic search and filtering operations without significant delay for the expected application size.
L43:- NFR-005: The system shall be maintainable, with clear separation between business logic, persistence, and user interface concerns.
L44:- NFR-006: The system shall be usable through a user interface that supports the required ticket management workflows.
L45:- NFR-007: The system shall behave deterministically for standard create, read, update, and search operations.
L46:
L47:## 5. Business Rules
L48:
L49:- BR-001: A ticket must include a title and description before it can be created or persistently saved.
L50:- BR-002: A ticket must have a valid priority value when the system accepts the update.
L51:- BR-003: A ticket may have an assignee or remain unassigned.Changing the assignee must be validated and persisted by the backend.
L52:- BR-004: Comments must be associated with an existing ticket.
L53:- BR-005: Ticket searches must operate on the ticket data currently stored in the system.
L54:- BR-006: Filtering by status must only return tickets that match the selected status value.
L55:- BR-007: Updates to ticket fields must be stored only after successful backend validation.
L56:- BR-008: The ticket lifecycle must remain coherent across create, update, list, and detail operations.
L57:- BR-009: The valid ticket state sequence is OPEN → IN_PROGRESS → RESOLVED → CLOSED.
L58:- BR-010: The system shall allow OPEN → CANCELLED and IN_PROGRESS → CANCELLED as valid terminal transitions.
L59:- BR-011: Any transition outside the defined state machine is invalid and must be rejected by the backend.
L60:- BR-012: The backend must enforce the state machine and must not rely on the frontend to determine valid transitions.
L61:- BR-013: Every newly created ticket shall have status `OPEN`.
L62:
L63:## 6. Validation Requirements
L64:
L65:- VR-001: The system shall reject empty or missing required ticket fields such as title and description.
L66:- VR-002: The system shall reject invalid ticket priority values that are not recognized by the supported priority model.
L67:- VR-003: If an assignee is provided, it shall conform to the assignee representation defined in the data model and API contract.
L68:- VR-004: The system shall reject invalid comment payloads or comments attached to unknown tickets.
L69:- VR-005: Search terms shall be trimmed before processing. A blank search term shall be treated as no search filter.
L70:- VR-006: A status filter shall accept only one of the supported ticket status values: OPEN, IN_PROGRESS, RESOLVED, CLOSED, or CANCELLED.
L71:- VR-007: The system shall validate all backend requests before changing system state or persisting data.
L72:- VR-008: The system shall validate ticket status transitions against the defined backend state machine before allowing a change.
L73:- VR-009: The system shall reject CLOSED → OPEN, RESOLVED → OPEN, and CANCELLED → OPEN as invalid transitions.
L74:
L75:## 7. Error-Handling Requirements
L76:
L77:- ER-001: The system shall return a meaningful error when a requested ticket does not exist.
L78:- ER-002: The system shall return a meaningful error when required input is missing or invalid.
L79:- ER-003: The system shall return a meaningful error when a comment cannot be added because the parent ticket is invalid or missing.
L80:- ER-004: The system shall return a meaningful error when a persistence or database operation fails.
L81:- ER-005: The system shall surface user-friendly error messages in the UI rather than exposing raw internal system errors.
L82:- ER-006: The system shall handle validation failures without corrupting ticket data.
L83:- ER-007: The system shall keep error handling consistent across all ticket operations.
L84:- ER-008: The system shall return a clear business-rule error when an attempted status transition is not allowed.
L85:- ER-009: Invalid status transitions shall be represented consistently as a `409 Conflict` response and shall not modify the ticket.
L86:
L87:## 8. Acceptance Criteria
L88:
L89:- AC-001: A user can create a ticket with valid data and the ticket is persisted in the database.
L90:- AC-002: A user can list tickets and view the ticket details of an existing record.
L91:- AC-003: A user can update a ticket title, description, priority, and assignee with valid input.
L92:- AC-004: A user can add a comment to an existing ticket successfully.
L93:- AC-005: A user can search tickets using a keyword and obtain matching results.
L94:- AC-006: A user can filter tickets by status and obtain only the records matching that status.
L95:- AC-007: Invalid input is rejected on the backend and the user sees a meaningful error message.
L96:- AC-008: The system persists ticket and comment data across operations without losing data integrity.
L97:- AC-009: The system provides a usable user interface for the described support ticket workflows.
L98:- AC-010: A ticket can move through the valid state sequence OPEN → IN_PROGRESS → RESOLVED → CLOSED.
L99:- AC-011: A ticket can transition from OPEN to CANCELLED or from IN_PROGRESS to CANCELLED.
L100:- AC-012: The backend rejects every status transition not defined as valid, including CLOSED → OPEN, RESOLVED → OPEN, CANCELLED → OPEN,OPEN → RESOLVED, OPEN → CLOSED, and other unsupported transitions.
L101:- AC-013: A newly created ticket has status `OPEN`.
L102:- AC-014: Ticket and comment data remains available after the application is stopped and restarted.
L103:
L104:## 9. Explicit Assumptions
L105:
L106:- AS-001: The application is a support ticket management system for managing issue records and comments.
L107:- AS-002: Ticket status is a core field that may be used for filtering and lifecycle tracking, even though the README does not define all available states.
L108:- AS-003: Ticket priority is a supported field but the README does not specify the exact allowed values; the system must define a valid set as part of the business rules.
L109:- AS-004: An assignee is represented as a user or stakeholder associated with a ticket, but the application may use a simplified representation unless otherwise specified.
L110:- AS-005: The UI is expected to display errors meaningfully, while the backend remains the source of validation and business enforcement.
L111:- AS-006: The system is intended to be a general-purpose small support ticket application rather than a large enterprise workflow system.
L112:- AS-007: PostgreSQL shall be supported as the primary persistent   database, and H2 may be used for tests or lightweight local development where appropriate.
L113:- AS-008: The README defines the ticket state machine as required business behavior and therefore the backend must enforce it even if the frontend allows a different flow.
L114:- AS-009: Invalid transitions are not accepted under any circumstance and must be rejected before persisting state changes.
L115:
L116:## 10. Out of Scope
L117:
L118:The following capabilities are not required unless explicitly added
L119:to the approved requirements:
L120:
L121:- User registration
L122:- Authentication
L123:- Authorization and role management
L124:- Email notifications
L125:- File attachments
L126:- Ticket deletion
L127:- Ticket history/audit logging
L128:- SLA management
L129:- Real-time notifications
L130:- External integrations
L131:- Full assignee/user management
```

L23:export default function TicketStatusActions({ ticket, onStatusChanged }: TicketStatusActionsProps) {

L33:      return;

L37:    setErrorMessage(null);
L38:    try {

  44-### 3.3 Constraints
  45-
  46-- `id` must be unique and not null.

  80-- Index on `priority` if priority-based queries or reporting are expected.
  81-- Index on `created_at` for listing and sorting by newest or oldest tickets.

  83:- Optional full-text or trigram index on `title` and `description` for keyword search, if the application needs more advanced text search.

  85-### 3.6 Design decisions
  86-
  87-- `status` is stored as a string or enum-backed value because the lifecycle is explicit and simple to validate.
  88:- `assignee` is intentionally flexible in this specification to allow either a direct user identifier or a textual representation, depending on implementation choice.
  89-- `created_at` and `updated_at` provide auditing and sorting support.
  90-- `closed_at` and `cancelled_at` capture when a ticket reached a terminal state, which helps with reporting and state clarity.

L1:# Ticket State Machine
L2:
L3:## 1. States
L4:    
L5:
L6:The ticket lifecycle includes the following states:
L7:
L8:- OPEN
L9:- IN_PROGRESS
L10:- RESOLVED
L11:- CLOSED
L12:- CANCELLED
L13:
L14:## 1.1 Initial state
L15:
L16:Every newly created ticket shall have the initial status:
L17:- OPEN
L18:The client shall not be required to provide an initial status when creating a ticket.
L19:
L20:## 1.2 Terminal states
L21:
L22:The following are terminal states:
L23:
L24:- CLOSED
L25:- CANCELLED
L26:
L27:A ticket in a terminal state cannot transition to any other state.
L28:
L29:## 2. Valid transitions
L30:
L31:The following transitions are valid:
L32:
L33:- OPEN -> IN_PROGRESS
L34:- IN_PROGRESS -> RESOLVED
L35:- RESOLVED -> CLOSED
L36:- OPEN -> CANCELLED
L37:- IN_PROGRESS -> CANCELLED
L38:
L39:The system must allow only these transitions. Every other transition is invalid.
L40:
L41:## 3. Invalid transition examples
L42:
L43:The backend must reject the following transitions:
L44:
L45:- CLOSED -> OPEN
L46:- RESOLVED -> OPEN
L47:- CANCELLED -> OPEN
L48:- OPEN -> RESOLVED
L49:- OPEN -> CLOSED
L50:- IN_PROGRESS -> OPEN
L51:- IN_PROGRESS -> CLOSED
L52:- RESOLVED -> IN_PROGRESS
L53:- RESOLVED -> CANCELLED
L54:- CLOSED -> IN_PROGRESS
L55:- CLOSED -> RESOLVED
L56:- CLOSED -> CANCELLED
L57:- CANCELLED -> IN_PROGRESS
L58:- CANCELLED -> RESOLVED
L59:- CANCELLED -> CLOSED
L60:- A ticket must not transition directly from OPEN to CLOSED.
L61:- A ticket must not transition directly from IN_PROGRESS to CLOSED.
L62:- CLOSED can only be reached from RESOLVED.
L63:
L64:Any transition not explicitly listed as valid must be rejected.
L65:
L66:## 4. Business rule summary
L67:
L68:- The normal lifecycle progresses forward from OPEN to IN_PROGRESS,then RESOLVED, then CLOSED.
L69:- Cancellation provides an alternative terminal path from OPEN or IN_PROGRESS.
L70:- Tickets may be cancelled only from OPEN or IN_PROGRESS.
L71:- Once a ticket reaches a terminal status such as CLOSED or CANCELLED, it must not transition back to an earlier state.
L72:- The backend is the source of truth for transition validation.
L73:- The frontend must not be trusted to enforce or determine valid transitions.
L74:
L75:## 5. Expected API behaviour
L76:
L77:- Any API endpoint that updates ticket status must validate the requested transition server-side.
L78:- Transition validation must occur in the backend before persistence.
L79:- If the requested transition is invalid, the API must reject the change and return an error response.
L80:- A valid transition must persist the new state and return the updated ticket information or a success response consistent with the API contract.
L81:- All status-changing API paths must use the same transition validation logic.
L82:
L83:## 6. Expected HTTP status for invalid transitions
L84:
L85:For invalid ticket status transitions, the API should use a client-error status code. Recommended status:
L86:
L87:- 409 Conflict
L88:
L89:Rationale:
L90:- The request conflicts with the current ticket state and the defined workflow rules.
L91:- A 400 Bad Request may also be used in some API designs, but 409 Conflict is the clearest and most semantically appropriate choice for invalid lifecycle transitions.
L92:
L93:The final status code used by the API should remain consistent across all ticket state-changing endpoints.
L94:
L95:## 7. Test cases
L96:
L97:### 7.1 Valid transition tests
L98:
L99:- TC-000: A newly created ticket has status OPEN.
L100:- TC-001: OPEN -> IN_PROGRESS is accepted.
L101:- TC-002: IN_PROGRESS -> RESOLVED is accepted.
L102:- TC-003: RESOLVED -> CLOSED is accepted.
L103:- TC-004: OPEN -> CANCELLED is accepted.
L104:- TC-005: IN_PROGRESS -> CANCELLED is accepted.
L105:
L106:### 7.2 Invalid transition tests
L107:
L108:- TC-006: CLOSED -> OPEN is rejected.
L109:- TC-007: RESOLVED -> OPEN is rejected.
L110:- TC-008: CANCELLED -> OPEN is rejected.
L111:- TC-009: OPEN -> RESOLVED is rejected.
L112:- TC-010: OPEN -> CLOSED is rejected.
L113:- TC-011: IN_PROGRESS -> OPEN is rejected.
L114:- TC-012: IN_PROGRESS -> CLOSED is rejected.
L115:- TC-013: RESOLVED -> IN_PROGRESS is rejected.
L116:- TC-014: RESOLVED -> CANCELLED is rejected.
L117:- TC-015: CLOSED -> IN_PROGRESS is rejected.
L118:- TC-016: CLOSED -> RESOLVED is rejected.
L119:- TC-017: CLOSED -> CANCELLED is rejected.
L120:- TC-018: CANCELLED -> IN_PROGRESS is rejected.
L121:- TC-019: CANCELLED -> RESOLVED is rejected.
L122:- TC-020: CANCELLED -> CLOSED is rejected.
L123:
L124:### 7.3 Business rule tests
L125:
L126:- TC-021: A terminal state cannot transition back to any earlier state.
L127:- TC-022: A ticket in CANCELLED state cannot transition to another status.
L128:- TC-023: A ticket in CLOSED state cannot transition to another status.
L129:- TC-024: A status-changing API request with a disallowed transition is rejected before persistence.
L130:- TC-025: A valid status change persists the new state and the updated state is readable afterward.
L131:
L132:### 7.4 API contract tests
L133:
L134:- TC-026: Valid transitions return the expected success response and updated ticket state.
L135:- TC-027: Invalid transitions return a consistent error payload and HTTP 409 status.
L136:- TC-028: All status-changing endpoints enforce the same state machine rules.
L137:
L138:## 8. Scope note
L139:
L140:This document defines the required ticket lifecycle and validation rules for the application. It is intended as a project-wide business rule specification and does not prescribe implementation code or framework-specific patterns.

L1:# Architecture Specification
L2:
L3:## 1. Overview
L4:
L5:This project is a small support ticket management system built with Java 21 and Spring Boot on the backend, a React/Next.js frontend, and PostgreSQL as the production database. The architecture is intentionally simple and pragmatic, with clear boundaries between the presentation layer, business logic, persistence, and external integration points.
L6:
L7:The design must remain appropriate to the size and complexity of the application. It should favor clarity and maintainability over unnecessary abstraction or framework-heavy patterns.
L8:
L9:## 2. Technology summary
L10:
L11:- Backend: Java 21, Spring Boot
L12:- Production database: PostgreSQL
L13:- Test/local lightweight database: H2
L14:- API: REST
L15:- Frontend: React/Next.js
L16:- Runtime model: a small, layered web application with clear service boundaries
L17:
L18:## 3. Backend architecture
L19:
L20:### 3.1 Layering
L21:
L22:The backend should follow a simple layered structure appropriate for a small application:
L23:
L24:- API/presentation layer
L25:  - Handles HTTP requests and responses
L26:  - Maps request payloads to application objects or DTOs
L27:  - Executes basic request validation and error translation
L28:  - Does not contain business rules
L29:
L30:- Application/service layer
L31:  - Contains use-case orchestration and business workflows
L32:  - Applies business rules and validation that are required by the application
L33:  - Coordinates persistence and domain behavior
L34:  - Owns transaction boundaries for write operations
L35:
L36:- Domain layer
L37:  - Holds core business concepts and rules when they add meaningful value
L38:  - Encapsulates state transitions and workflow logic
L39:  - Keeps business rules out of controllers and repositories
L40:  - May be lightweight for a small application, but must still protect invariants and valid state transitions
L41:
L42:- Persistence/infrastructure layer
L43:  - Manages database access, repositories, and technical integration concerns
L44:  - Isolates persistence technology from higher layers
L45:  - Exposes data access capabilities without leaking technical details into the business layer
L46:
L47:### 3.2 Backend responsibilities
L48:
L49:- Expose REST endpoints for ticket operations
L50:- Validate incoming requests
L51:- Enforce business rules and state transitions
L52:- Coordinate persistence and transactional writes
L53:- Return consistent success and error responses
L54:- Keep controllers thin and focused on HTTP concerns
L55:
L56:### 3.3 Business rule ownership
L57:
L58:- The domain model owns ticket lifecycle invariants and valid state transitions.
L59:- The application/service layer coordinates use cases, transactions,authorization boundaries if introduced later, and persistence.
L60:- The service layer must not duplicate the state-machine rules when those rules are already enforced by the domain model.
L61:- Controllers must not implement state-machine logic.
L62:
L63:## 4. Frontend architecture
L64:
L65:The frontend should be intentionally lightweight and focused on user experience and interaction with the backend API.
L66:
L67:### 4.1 Frontend responsibilities
L68:
L69:- Render ticket-related pages and forms
L70:- Collect user input and submit requests to the backend
L71:- Display ticket lists, detail views, and status-aware UI states
L72:- Show meaningful validation and failure messages to users
L73:- Provide a user-friendly interface for ticket lifecycle actions
L74:
L75:### 4.2 Frontend constraints
L76:
L77:- The frontend must not be treated as the source of truth for business rules.
L78:- The frontend may provide UI guidance and convenience checks, but the backend is authoritative for validation and workflow enforcement.
L79:- The frontend should not duplicate complex business logic or state-machine rules that belong to the backend.
L80:- Frontend behavior should remain simple and aligned with the API contract.
L81:
L82:## 5. Database boundary
L83:
L84:### 5.1 Production database
L85:
L86:- PostgreSQL is the production database.
L87:- It is used for persistent application data and transactional consistency.
L88:- The database should maintain the canonical state of ticket records and related data.
L89:
L90:### 5.2 Test/local database
L91:
L92:- H2 may be used for fast unit/integration tests where the SQL and persistence behavior are compatible with PostgreSQL.
L93:- Tests that depend on PostgreSQL-specific behavior shall use a PostgreSQL test environment rather than relying on H2 compatibility.
L94:- H2 shall not be treated as behaviorally identical to PostgreSQL.
L95:
L96:### 5.3 Persistence boundaries
L97:
L98:- Persistence concerns belong in the repository/infrastructure layer.
L99:- Application logic should not depend on database implementation details.
L100:- JPA entities may be used for persistence models when appropriate, but they should not be exposed directly as API contracts.
L101:
L102:## 6. API boundary
L103:
L104:The application exposes a REST API that is the contract between frontend and backend.
L105:
L106:### 6.1 API responsibilities
L107:
L108:- Define resource-oriented endpoints for ticket operations
L109:- Use standard HTTP methods and semantics
L110:- Return consistent success and error payloads
L111:- Validate input at the API boundary
L112:- Translate backend exceptions into clear HTTP responses
L113:
L114:### 6.2 API constraints
L115:
L116:- The API contract must remain separate from persistence entities and internal domain models.
L117:- Controllers should not contain business logic.
L118:- API responses should avoid leaking internal implementation details.
L119:- DTOs should represent the public contract, not persistence structure.
L120:
L121:## 7. Validation boundary
L122:
L123:Validation should occur at clear boundaries:
L124:
L125:- API boundary: validate incoming request structure, required fields, and obvious format errors
L126:- Service/application layer: validate business rules and workflow constraints
L127:- Persistence/database layer: enforce data integrity constraints when needed
L128:
L129:The backend must enforce all meaningful validation rules. The frontend may help with UX, but it is not the authoritative validation layer.
L130:
L131:## 8. State-machine responsibility
L132:
L133:The ticket state machine is a core business rule and must be enforced by the backend.
L134:
L135:### 8.1 Required lifecycle
L136:
L137:- Newly created tickets shall start in the OPEN state.
L138:- The client shall not control the initial lifecycle state during ticket creation.
L139:
L140:- OPEN -> IN_PROGRESS
L141:- IN_PROGRESS -> RESOLVED
L142:- RESOLVED -> CLOSED
L143:- OPEN -> CANCELLED
L144:- IN_PROGRESS -> CANCELLED
L145:
L146:### 8.2 Enforcement requirement
L147:
L148:- The backend is the source of truth for valid ticket transitions.
L149:- The frontend must not determine whether a transition is valid.
L150:- All API paths that can change ticket status must use the same transition validation logic.
L151:- Invalid transitions must be rejected before persistence.
L152:
L153:### 8.3 Terminal states
L154:
L155:- CLOSED and CANCELLED are terminal states in the defined state machine.
L156:- A ticket in a terminal state must not transition back to an earlier state.
L157:
L158:## 9. Error handling
L159:
L160:Errors should be handled in a consistent, predictable way across the application.
L161:
L162:### 9.1 Backend error handling
L163:
L164:- Translate validation failures, domain violations, and persistence failures into clear API responses.
L165:- Return meaningful error messages without exposing internal system details.
L166:- Use consistent HTTP status codes for similar failures.
L167:- Keep exception handling centralized at the HTTP boundary where practical.
L168:
L169:### 9.2 Frontend error handling
L170:
L171:- Render meaningful user-facing errors based on API responses.
L172:- Display validation feedback and failure messages without exposing internal technical details.
L173:- Keep error rendering simple and user-friendly.
L174:
L175:## 10. Testing architecture
L176:
L177:The testing strategy should remain lean and practical for a small application.
L178:
L179:### 10.1 Test layers
L180:
L181:- Unit tests
L182:  - Validate focused business logic and validation behavior
L183:  - Keep tests fast and isolated
L184:
L185:- Integration tests
L186:  - Validate interactions across key application components and persistence
L187:  - Use controlled data and environment setup
L188:
L189:- API tests
L190:  - Validate HTTP contracts, status codes, payloads, and error responses
L191:
L192:- Repository/persistence tests
L193:  - Verify query behavior and persistence semantics where needed
L194:
L195:### 10.2 Rules
L196:
L197:- Tests should validate real behavior rather than mock internals.
L198:- Use mocks only where external dependencies or constraints require them.
L199:- Avoid brittle or over-engineered test patterns.
L200:- Keep the test suite maintainable and fast enough for normal development feedback.
L201:
L202:## 11. Configuration and environment strategy
L203:
L204:### 11.1 Environment separation
L205:
L206:- Use environment-specific configuration for application settings.
L207:- Keep local development, testing, and production configuration clearly separated.
L208:- Use environment variables or external configuration for secrets and sensitive values.
L209:
L210:### 11.2 Database configuration
L211:
L212:- PostgreSQL for production and any shared or full deployment environment.
L213:- H2 for local execution and lightweight tests when appropriate.
L214:- Avoid hard-coding credentials or sensitive configuration values in source-controlled files.
L215:
L216:### 11.3 Operational configuration
L217:
L218:- Keep configuration explicit and readable.
L219:- Prefer standard Spring Boot conventions over custom configuration patterns.
L220:- Keep the environment setup simple and suitable for a small application.
L221:
L222:## 12. Design principles for a small application
L223:
L224:- Favor a simple layered architecture over speculative abstraction.
L225:- Add a dedicated domain layer only when it meaningfully improves the understanding or enforcement of business rules.
L226:- Avoid creating layers or abstractions solely to satisfy a pattern.
L227:- Prefer clear responsibilities and straightforward code over generic frameworks.
L228:- Keep the system easy to understand, test, and evolve.
L229:
L230:## 13. Scope note
L231:
L232:This architecture is intended for a small support ticket management system. It balances clarity, maintainability, and project size without introducing unnecessary complexity or heavy enterprise patterns.
L233:
